title: Southern Delta Aquariids Meteor Shower
direction: Look south toward Aquarius after midnight
description: A steady meteor shower with long glowing streaks. Good warm-up before Perseids.
tips: Best after midnight under dark skies.

title: Alpha Capricornids Meteor Shower
direction: Look toward Capricornus
description: Not huge in number, but famous for slow, dramatic fireball meteors.
tips: Watch from dark skies for the brightest fireballs.

title: Saturn at Opposition
direction: Rises in east at sunset
description: Saturn becomes brightest and closest for the year. Rings clearly visible in a telescope.
tips: Even binoculars help; telescope gives the best wow factor.

title: Total Solar Eclipse
visibility: Best from Greenland, Iceland, Spain; partial elsewhere
direction: Look toward the Sun ONLY with proper eclipse protection
description: The Moon completely covers the Sun for observers in the path of totality.
tips: Never observe without certified solar eclipse glasses.

title: Perseid Meteor Shower
direction: Look northeast toward Perseus
description: One of the most spectacular annual meteor showers, caused by debris from Comet Swift-Tuttle.
tips: No telescope needed. Best after midnight.

title: Partial Lunar Eclipse
direction: Look at the Moon
description: Earth's shadow partially covers the Moon, creating a dramatic dark bite.
tips: Safe to observe with naked eyes or binoculars.

title: September Equinox
direction: Observe sunrise due east / sunset due west
description: Day and night become approximately equal in length worldwide.
tips: Fun date for shadow and solar angle observations.

title: Draconid Meteor Shower
direction: Look north toward Draco
description: Usually modest, but occasionally produces surprise outbursts.
tips: One of the rare showers good in evening hours.

title: Orionid Meteor Shower
direction: Look toward Orion after midnight
description: Fast meteors created by debris from Halley's Comet.
tips: Best after midnight until dawn.

title: Delta Aquarid Meteor Shower
direction: Look toward Aquarius constellation in the south
description: A reliable midsummer shower that overlaps with the early Perseids. Long, slow meteors with glowing trails are its signature. Best from southern latitudes but worth watching anywhere.
tips: Pair this with early Perseids for a rich viewing night.

title: June Solstice
direction: Watch the sunrise — it reaches its northernmost point on the horizon
description: The Sun reaches its northernmost point in the sky. The longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere, and the shortest in the Southern. Many ancient sites like Stonehenge were aligned for this exact moment.
tips: Sunrise and sunset are at their most extreme positions on the horizon today.

title: Orionid Meteor Shower
direction: Look toward Orion's raised arm (northeast)
description: These meteors are shed by Halley's Comet — some of the fastest and brightest of any shower, often leaving persistent glowing trails. Orion rises around midnight so the best views are after 1 AM.
tips: Halley's debris hits the atmosphere at 66 km/s — expect brilliant streaks.

title: Leonid Meteor Shower
direction: Look toward Leo constellation in the east
description: Famous for producing dramatic meteor storms every 33 years when Earth passes through dense debris from comet Tempel-Tuttle. In off-storm years it's still a reliable mid-autumn show with fast, bright meteors.
tips: Best after midnight when Leo is well above the horizon.

title: Geminid Meteor Shower
direction: Radiant near Castor in Gemini — look northeast
description: The Geminids are the king of annual meteor showers. Unusually, they originate from an asteroid (3200 Phaethon) rather than a comet. Multi-colored meteors including white, yellow, green, and red. Gemini rises early so you can watch from 9 PM onward.
tips: This is the one to not miss. Bundle up — December skies are cold but usually clear.

title: Winter Solstice
direction: Watch the sunset — it sets at its most southwesterly point today
description: The shortest day in the Northern Hemisphere and the beginning of astronomical winter. The Sun reaches its lowest arc across the sky. After today, days slowly grow longer.
tips: A great night for stargazing — 16+ hours of darkness at northern latitudes.

title: Ursid Meteor Shower
direction: Look toward Ursa Minor (Little Dipper) in the north
description: A modest but charming Christmas-season shower. Debris from comet 8P/Tuttle. Conveniently coincides with the winter solstice and is circumpolar — the radiant never sets for northern viewers.
tips: Low rates but a lovely backdrop for a cold December night.

title: Quadrantid Meteor Shower
direction: Look north toward Boötes / Draco border
description: The first major shower of the year and potentially the strongest. Its peak lasts only a few hours, so timing is critical. Originates from asteroid 2003 EH1, thought to be an extinct comet.
tips: The peak is short — check your local time carefully and be outside 30 min early.

title: Lyrid Meteor Shower
direction: Look toward Lyra constellation near Vega
description: One of the oldest recorded meteor showers, observed for over 2,700 years. Debris from comet Thatcher. Occasional outbursts can push rates to 100/hr. Bright moonless years produce spectacular shows.
tips: The shower is active before dawn. Vega rises around midnight.

title: Eta Aquarid Meteor Shower
direction: Look east toward Aquarius before dawn
description: These are Halley's Comet meteors entering from the north. In the Southern Hemisphere, rates can hit 50/hr. From northern latitudes it's a more modest show, but the meteors that do appear are fast with long glowing tails.
tips: Best views are in the 2 hours before dawn.

title: Neptune at Opposition
direction: Look in Pisces constellation, low in the east after sunset
description: Neptune reaches its closest point to Earth for 2026. At magnitude 7.8 it's not visible to the naked eye, but binoculars will reveal a blue-green 'star' that doesn't twinkle. A telescope shows its characteristic blue disk.
tips: Use binoculars or a telescope. Neptune looks like a pale blue dot.

title: Jupiter at Opposition
direction: Rises in the east at sunset, highest around midnight in Taurus
description: Jupiter at its brightest and biggest of 2026. At magnitude -2.9 it outshines everything except Venus and the Moon. Even binoculars show the four Galilean moons. A small telescope reveals the cloud bands and the Great Red Spot.
tips: The four Galilean moons shift positions night to night — it's fascinating to track them.
